A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same unified motion synthesis/comprehension research, renamed from MotionLLaMA to VersatileMotion. The complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables and equations, support comparison despite substantial methodological revisions.

before.justification: V1 reports original MotionLLaMA benchmark results, tokenizer reconstruction experiments and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix C.

after.justification: V2 reports original VersatileMotion and FlowVQ results, generalist/specialist comparisons, initialization experiments and extensive tokenizer ablations in Section 5 and Appendices B–C.

M1.justification: HoMi's separate hand/body encoders and Fourier gating are replaced by FSQ-based FlowVQ with an iterative Flow Matching decoder. V2 also introduces sequential generalist pretraining, reply-only generalist tuning and specialist tuning, replacing v1's two-stage strategy. Optional compound conditions extend the motion-message procedure.

E1.justification: MotionHub substantially expands its training coverage with sources including NTU-RGBD-120, UESTC and TED (v1 Table 10; v2 Table 2). V2 also evaluates combined audio/text conditioning qualitatively in Figure 5. The nine core benchmark task families remain, and empirical multi-agent evaluation still concerns two people.

E2.justification: V2 adds Lodge to music-to-dance comparisons and MDM to multi-agent text-to-motion, while removing MCM from single-agent text-to-motion. Its main reconstruction comparison adds Motion FSQ-VAE and drops MoVQ and standalone RVQ rows; RVQ remains evaluated in appendix ablations. These alter comparator membership across several retained experiments.

E3.justification: Reported training budgets change from v1's 500-epoch pretraining/instruction-tuning setting to 30 pretraining, 30 generalist-tuning and 100 specialist-tuning epochs in v2 Appendix A. V2 adds controlled 10-epoch initialization comparisons across 1B–8B backbones. Reconstruction tables also report PA-MPJPE instead of N-MPJPE. These are substantive reported setting changes.

E4.justification: V1 already studies motion representations, codebook size and HoMi components. V2 replaces the HoMi-component ablation with FlowVQ reconstruction/downstream ablations and adds training-stage and initialization/scale analyses. Appendices B–C greatly expand tokenizer investigations, including standardization, dilation, quantizer choice, depth, causal convolutions, patchification and training-clip length.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2's standard-deviation formulas concern input normalization, not uncertainty in experimental results.

E6.justification: Benchmark results are extensively replaced and supplemented with generalist, specialist and FlowVQ rows. For example, v1 Table 3 reports T2M FID 0.0268 versus MCM's 0.0179; v2 Table 4 reports 62.8245 for specialist+FlowVQ versus MoMask's 76.0154, the best listed external comparator. These are results under revised conditions, not a same-setting performance gain. Numerous new ablation results also appear.

T1.justification: V2 Section 4.2 adds mathematical definitions of noisy motion, conditioned velocity prediction and the residual-field loss in Equations 3–5. These formal additions are localized to the new decoder. Existing R-precision, BAS and F1 definitions are retained in the relocated metrics appendix; neither version develops theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: V1 centers its contributions on HoMi's single-codebook reconstruction and SOTA performance in completion, interaction generation and comprehension. V2 centers FlowVQ, generalist-to-specialist training and standardized MotionHub benchmarks, claiming SOTA on seven of nine tasks. This substantially redefines the principal methodological contributions and performance claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking generalist pretraining to benefits on data-scarce interaction tasks and linking quantizer effectiveness to encoder quality. It discusses computational tradeoffs behind tokenizer choices. Appendix F newly acknowledges that caption granularity is not explicitly exploited and that arbitrary-agent architectural support has only been validated on two-person interactions.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix A adds detailed architectures, optimizer settings, GPU resources, training times, precision, distributed-training tools, flow-sampling steps and missing-hand loss handling. However, v1's explicit repository link and inference temperature/top-p settings disappear; v2 describes the MMotion codebase without providing its access link. Documentation is substantially expanded but retains gaps.

R1.justification: V2 expands positioning around quantization bottlenecks, scalable motion models and reconstruction versus generation quality. Newly incorporated works include ScaMo, Finite Scalar Quantization, The Language of Motion, MotionGPT-2, Cosmos and the optimization-dilemma study. These support a substantially revised methodological framing rather than merely updated bibliography formatting.

P1.justification: The paper is renamed, and the abstract, introduction, contribution narrative and method description are extensively rewritten around FlowVQ and generalist/specialist training. MotionHub moves from the appendix into a dedicated main-text section, implementation details move into Appendix A, and the appendices are substantially reorganized and expanded.

P2.justification: V2 adopts an ACM journal layout, adds a new teaser, redraws the framework/tokenizer diagrams and introduces baseline-comparison and compound-conditioning visuals. Tables gain generalist/specialist/FlowVQ rows, and music-to-dance and dance-to-music comparisons are merged. V1 Figure 1 is retained as v2 Appendix Figure 6, while the codebook-utilization plot disappears.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the unified-training contribution: Tables 11–12 isolate training-stage effects that v1 did not test, while tokenizer ablations establish which design choices matter. Appendix A greatly improves implementation documentation, and Appendix F clarifies applicability limits. These gains outweigh the removed repository link and MCM T2M comparison. Unspecified benchmark splits and remaining overstatements, such as the S2G FGD claim despite MCM's better value in Table 9, still limit confidence in some conclusions.
